u0531: How to write AI art prompts for generating images
u0532: A good image starts with a clear idea.
u0533: Writing an AI art prompt is a way to turn that idea into a brief: what the subject is, where it belongs, how the light falls and what the picture should feel like. You can start with everyday language and add detail as your direction becomes clearer.
u0534: This guide walks through the building blocks of a prompt, practical ways to refine it and four examples you can adapt. When you are ready, open the
u0536: and choose the model and settings that fit your project.
u0538: An AI art prompt is a creative brief.
u0539: It tells an image model what you want to see: a subject, a setting, a composition and a visual direction. A useful brief describes the details that matter to the picture instead of collecting impressive-sounding words.
u0540: Think about the difference between “a portrait” and a portrait with a specific crop, expression and light. Both are valid starting points. The second gives you clearer details to review when an image appears. A prompt does not need to describe every leaf or thread; it needs to make your priorities understandable.
u0541: How do AI art generators work?
u0542: An image model uses your instructions to produce a visual interpretation. The selected model, the words you provide and the settings you choose all contribute to the result. A useful way to approach the process is to separate the brief from the controls and the review.
u0544: The prompt communicates what belongs in the scene and how it should feel. Concrete relationships help: a cup on a table, a person beside a window, or a mountain behind a lake. Explain which element should draw the eye first.
u0546: Aspect ratio, resolution and reference inputs depend on the selected model. Use the workspace’s resolution controls for output dimensions; writing “8K” into a sentence does not set the exported file size. A reference can help explain a direction when the chosen model supports it.
u0548: Check the result against your brief. Look at the framing, important details, unwanted objects and any text. Two generations can differ even with similar wording. Treat each result as a direction to inspect and refine, rather than assuming that a detailed sentence guarantees an exact picture.

u0554: How to write an AI art prompt
u0555: Start with a plain description of the image you actually need. For example, replace “a dog” with the kind of dog, what it is doing and where it is. Then add the few visual decisions that make this particular picture useful to you.
u0557: Name the main subject and describe its pose or activity. “A small white dog looking up from an open book” gives you a more useful focal point than a list of unrelated objects.
u0559: Say where the subject belongs and how the scene is arranged. Describe the foreground, background and any space you need to keep clear. A product image for a banner may need room beside the subject.
u0561: Choose a direction that fits the idea: soft window light, a cool night palette, warm sunset reflections or a cheerful illustrated garden. Keep the lighting description consistent with the setting.
u0563: Describe the medium or visual qualities you want, such as a watercolor illustration, a textured collage or a studio photograph. Specific qualities are easier to revise than a long stack of style labels.
u0565: Ask for a close-up, a wide view or a centered composition when it matters. Mention materials, expressions and shapes that need attention. Set the actual aspect ratio and output size in the controls offered by the selected model.
u0567: The most useful prompt is one you can understand, test and revise. Keep a clear relationship between the words you change and the part of the picture you want to improve. These habits make that process easier:
u0569: Write the subject and the important relationships plainly. “A red ceramic cup on a pale wooden table” is a clear starting point. Add specialist terms when they communicate a visual decision you can recognize in the result.
u0571: Decide what makes the image successful before adding decorative details. If the crop and expression matter most, describe them clearly. A longer prompt is useful only when the extra information serves the picture; there is no universal ideal word count.
u0573: Check for conflicting directions, such as an empty background filled with objects. You can combine styles deliberately, but explain the relationship rather than leaving the model to guess which instruction should dominate.
u0575: When you like the composition but want softer light, revise the lighting description first. Rewriting the subject, palette and framing at the same time makes it harder to learn which change helped.
u0577: Inspect the image closely for small errors, then check it in the crop where it will be used. A background that looks attractive full-screen may distract from a tiny profile image. Keep useful wording alongside the result so you can build on it.

u2183: The work happens on a canvas
u2184: Teams run close to a third of their image work inside Spaces. Individual accounts, less than a fifth. Teams also reach for standalone editing tools less often.
u2185: Not that teams edit less. That the editing stopped being a separate trip. On a canvas the reference, the prompt and every earlier version stay with the work, so the next person picks it up where the last one left it. At 50 images a week that compounds. At 2, it barely registers.
u2186: If more than one person touches the same image, start on the canvas and stay there. The tools are the same. What changes is whether the context survives between them.
u2188: Share of image work by surface, team vs individual paid accounts.
u2191: The most common edit isn't a tool. It's a sentence
u2192: When a generated image goes anywhere next, the most common destination isn't background removal or upscaling. It's another turn of conversation. More than half of all first steps after generating are a follow-up instruction, not a tool.
u2193: A toolbar assumes you already know which tool you need. Conversation doesn't. "Make the light colder" never mapped to a button, and now it doesn't have to. That's the shift: you describe the result, not the operation.
u2194: Say what's wrong with the image before deciding which tool fixes it. You'll usually find the tool wasn't the question.
u2195: The models people reach for first
u2196: These are the models most in demand on Magnific right now. Team accounts and individual accounts reach for almost exactly the same ones.
u2197: Range is the point, not a ranking. One model sets type cleanly. Another holds photographic skin. Another goes straight to 4K. You don't need all of them—you need the right one for the image in front of you.
u2198: In about 1 in 5 generations, the editor picks the model for you
u2199: Automatic selection reaches more distinct users than any individual model. Close to a fifth of all image generation runs with the model chosen for you.
u2200: Two populations, not one. Most people never open the model picker. A smaller group generates most of the images and chooses deliberately every time. Both are right. Picking a model pays off when you're producing at volume and know what each one does with typography, skin, or text. Below that, the choice costs more attention than it returns.
u2201: Stay on automatic until you can name what you'd change. Then the picker starts earning its place.
u2202: Teams change the resolution, not the model
u2203: Where resolution is chosen explicitly, 2K takes about half of all requests. Team accounts ask for 4K around 3 times more often than individual accounts—it's the setting that separates production work from everything else.
u2204: 2K is the working default because most output is screen output. 4K is a production decision, not a quality one: you reach for it when something gets cropped, printed, or composited at scale.
u2205: Generate at 2K while you're deciding. Go up once the image is the one.
u2207: Share of generations where resolution is chosen explicitly (about 43% of image generation). The rest carry no resolution.
u2208: How many tries it actually takes
u2209: The numbers run lower than most people guess. Prompting to a result isn't 100 attempts. It's a handful, and the sessions that run long are the ones deliberately exploring range.
u2210: Estimating credits for a project? Count sessions and multiply by a small number. Counting prompts overestimates badly.
u2211: When an image gets edited, it gets edited now
u2212: 3 out of 4 follow-up edits begin within 5 minutes. About 7 in 10 stop after a single step. Among tool-based edits, the first move is usually background removal, not upscaling.
u2213: One sitting, not a pipeline. And background-first says compositing: the image is going into something else, so it needs to come out of its rectangle before anything else matters.
u2220: Programmatic generation arrives through assistants and MCP clients. Among external agents, around 8 in 10 of it comes through Claude, with ChatGPT and coding tools making up most of the rest.
u2221: Programmatic image generation stopped requiring an integration project. It arrives through the assistant someone already has open, not through a build. That changes who can reach for it: from an engineering team to anyone with a connected tool.

u3395: What is an AI tattoo generator?
u3396: It helps turn a written tattoo idea into visual concepts. On this page you can describe the subject, style and intended placement, then continue to Epifera’s image generator to choose a model and create.
u3397: How does an AI tattoo generator work?
u3398: Your inputs become an editable creative brief. In the image generator you choose a model and its supported settings, review the cost and explicitly start generation. Filling this form does not create or charge for an image.
u3399: What should I include in an AI tattoo prompt?
u3400: Describe the subject, composition, style, colors and level of detail. You can also mention placement and approximate proportions. A clear starting idea is more useful than a long list of unrelated instructions.
u3401: Can I create a tattoo design from a photo, sketch, or reference image?
u3402: You can add an image in the image generator when the selected model supports references. This page prepares a text brief; image upload options and limits are shown in the workspace.
u3403: Can I control the tattoo’s style, colors, line weight, shading, size, and level of detail?
u3404: Include those details in the brief and refine them in later variations. Available settings depend on the selected model, and generated images may not follow every instruction exactly.
u3405: What tattoo styles can AI generate?
u3406: Try fine line, blackwork, old school, geometric, botanical or a style described in your own words. Presets are starting points, and you can edit the style field freely.
u3407: Can I design a tattoo for a specific body placement?
u3408: Add the intended placement to your brief to explore a suitable composition. It is a visual direction rather than a guarantee of anatomical fit, scale or final positioning.
u3409: Can I preview an AI tattoo on my own body?
u3410: An image-reference model may help explore a placement concept, depending on its supported inputs. Epifera does not provide a dedicated body-fitting or tattoo try-on tool on this page.
u3411: Are AI-generated tattoo designs suitable for real tattoos?
u3412: Treat a generated design as a concept. A tattoo artist should review and adapt the detail, line work, scale and placement before it becomes a finished tattoo design.
u3413: Can tattoo artists use the generator to create flash sheets or client concepts?
u3414: It can be used to explore visual ideas and compositions. Review and redraw the result as needed, check the applicable terms, and use only references you are entitled to use.
u3415: How do I refine a tattoo design that is close but not quite right?
u3416: Keep the parts of the brief that work and change the details you want to explore. If the selected model supports image references, you can use the previous result as a starting point for a new variation.
u3417: How do I share an AI-generated tattoo design with my tattoo artist?
u3418: Download a result from the workspace and share it together with your idea, preferred placement and approximate size. Your artist can then develop the final design.
u3419: Is the AI tattoo generator free to use?
u3420: Preparing a brief on this page does not start a paid job. Generation uses the selected model’s current pricing, shown in the workspace before you confirm. This page does not promise free or unlimited generations.
u3421: Who owns an AI-generated tattoo design?
u3422: Use of generated content is subject to Epifera’s terms and any applicable model conditions. This page does not promise exclusivity, copyright protection or that a design is unique. Review the terms before commercial use.
u3423: Are my uploaded photos, sketches, and body images private?
u3424: This page has no upload field. If you add references in the workspace, review Epifera’s data policy and avoid sharing personal or sensitive images unnecessarily. The relevant documents are available from the footer.
